title: Chapter 12 — The One Who Doesn't Stop
text:
The team is good. They don't bunch and they don't panic. They peel back to the SUVs and start working the angles, and good is the problem. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s read can stay ahead of one gun. Five at once is a cost, and every read he spends is gone for good. His nervous system starts to cook under the load.

A second slug catches the flanker breaking left, and the man drops mid-stride. A third punches through the door an operator is crouched behind and folds the steel in after it. A fourth catches a man rising from cover and puts him back down.

Then <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> runs dry on the fifth — the hammer falls on an empty chamber, a click he feels in his back teeth. No time to swing <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity> out and thumb in fresh rounds, so he stops solving the problem with the gun. He reaches over his shoulder and draws <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> off his back. The katana is a matte-black length of steel-CNT alloy, and the light doesn't come back off it — no piezo, no glow, no trick beyond the hand that holds it, and the hand has had eleven years to practice. He crosses the open ground inside the half-second his neuretics bought him, reads the man's weight and the angle of the shoulders three steps before the man commits to them, slides under the muzzle before it can track him, and lifts the rifle clean out of the fifth man's hands at the receiver. The gun spins away across the asphalt. The man is left disarmed, untouched, and loudly amazed to still have all ten fingers.

The sword for the problems steel can solve, <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> for the rest. Between them they have kept him alive longer than the odds allow. Behind his eyes the overclock runs hot — a high whine at the base of his skull that nobody else can hear, the hardware charging him for every read stacked on the last. A small red light ticks over at the corner of his sight, the way it always does when he pulls too much at once. His right hand trembles once against the grip, then stops. A thin line of blood starts from his nose; he thumbs it off his lip without thinking, and white creeps in at the edges of everything he can see. He ignores both. He's learned to. That's the whole trick of the debt — it doesn't take payment now. It waits, and it collects in some other form, some other moment, some choice he won't see coming until it's already written into his body.

Five down or out. One left — the leader, who hasn't moved this whole time, because the leader has been waiting.

The leader brought the weapon built for men like <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. He's only been waiting for the range to clear enough to use it. It's a Gauss rifle — a man-portable rail driver that throws a single hypersonic depleted-uranium dart along a line so flat it might as well be ruled with a straightedge, and it doesn't care what's standing behind the target. It's the one weapon <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics can't beat. You can't dodge a thing that's already past you. You can only try not to be standing where it was aimed.

He settles it on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s chest and fires. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reads the shot the breath before it leaves the barrel, and for that one breath the read hands him both outcomes at once. Stay in the line: take the dart clean through the sternum, dead or worse before the sound of it arrives — honest, finished, over. Or step, and let it go find whatever it finds instead. There is no version where nothing gets paid. He has known which one he'd choose since before he had words for who it was for: a workbench with six inches of clear space on it, a latch he's watched for months, a door across a hall that has stopped being locked to him. He steps.

The dart finds nothing but the air he left behind, and it doesn't stop. It crosses the intersection dead straight and punches through the windshield of an ambulance running north under its lights, and it takes the driver through the seat without slowing down to do it. He's dead before the vehicle knows it's lost him. With no one to steer, the ambulance drifts through its turn and meets a stalled hauler at fifty-two miles an hour. The impact throws its back doors wide on their hinges.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> does not look at the cab. He won't look at it tonight, or any night after. Later, going back over the count the way he goes back over every fight, he'll find the one place that stays blank, and he won't ask himself why.

He's inside the leader's reach before the man can cycle the rifle for a second shot. One clean upward cut, and the Gauss rifle clatters loose to start a quieter life on the pavement.

He straightens in the light of the wreck. Through the sprung-open bay doors of the ambulance, a small face is looking out at him. The small face lifts a hand and waves.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waves back.

"Are you the new one?" the small face asks.

She's eight, maybe nine. Her chest is taped under a flexible biopolymer brace, and she is, by a wide margin, calmer than the one-armed CorpoNation security officer bleeding out on the asphalt a yard to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left.

He steps up into the bay. The interior is a catalog of restraint systems and transport gear, all of it designed for a trip that never finished. The driver is slumped forward against the wheel. Dead. The medic in the passenger seat isn't coming back either, one arm trailing toward the floor, eyes open to nothing. Neither of them had time to know what was coming.

The kid has the faint iridescence of expensive genetic work — not the visible chrome of corpo-tier augmentation, but the deep cellular kind, the kind that costs before you're born. The patient tag clipped to the gurney reads IMANI OKONKWO-LINDQVIST — CRUCIBLE GENOMICS RECIPIENT — POST-OP, FIRST 6 HOURS — NORTHWESTERN MEMORIAL. Crucible Genomics prints organs to order. So the kid is six hours into living on one of them, and both of the people keeping her alive are dead. He reads the tag twice. It comes to one thing, and the one thing is bad.

The monitors above the gurney are running off battery now, their numbers scrolling downward in a slow, steady count.

"Hi, Imani," he says. "I'm <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

"I know," she says. "My uncle <entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity> says you're the one who doesn't stop."

He thumbs the emergency contact on the tag. His overlay chimes once — the tag going out on the emergency medical band.

"Pike," a voice says, already moving.

"Your driver's dead," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. "The kid's on the floor of a south-side ditch with a bioprinted heart wired to a battery. I have a motorcycle."

A pause — not shock, recognition. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." Pike says it flat, the way you say the name of a problem you already know by heart. "Of course it's you."

"What's the brace reading?" Pike asks.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looks. "Sinus, ninety-two, paced."

"You've got sixty minutes before the vascular scaffold throws a clot," Pike says. "Maybe seventy."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> doesn't hear the maybe. The same neuretics that read the kill team a hundred and twenty milliseconds ahead of itself read the brace now — the battery draw, the kid's color, the plain hard fact of a six-hour-old heart, the print quality already degrading the way the fabricators never advertise — and give him back one number, cold, with no maybe in it. Sixty.

"Keep her calm," Pike is saying. "A new graft that races can tear right off the suture line. Those wires aren't there for decoration."

"Northwestern?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asks.

"Streeterville. Trauma Bay Nine. I'll have a slot waiting — they'll prep the OR knowing what's coming through the door."

"I'm in Hegewisch."

Pike gets there almost as fast as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics had. "Then it's a straight line. North. Don't stop for checkpoints, don't stop for anything. And mind The Weather — there's a schism parked over 35th, has been since Tuesday, and your straight line runs right under it. Category 1, stable, but stable's the word that lies to you. If the read in your skull drops out, you're in it. Your neuretics will want to map the distortion. Don't let them. Steady speed — not faster, not slower, the edges pull either way — eyes on a far light, and whatever you do, don't look sideways. The moment you try to understand what you're looking at, you're gone."

"See you in a few," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says.

The connection drops.

He lifts <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> onto the back of the seat, sidesaddle, and threads the medical harness through his belt loop so the battery rides snug over his kidney instead of swinging loose. He ties her wrists loosely through the back of his coat so she won't fall if she sleeps. Then he loads <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> with a fresh moon-clip — six rounds, a full wheel, to replace the four he'd spent back at the Hegewisch crossroads — and lets it settle on his left hip. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> rides across his back. He needs to reach Trauma Bay Nine before the scaffold throws its clot — sixty minutes, no maybe in it, and twenty-two miles of city between Hegewisch and Streeterville on roads that will not be clear.

Her cheek finds the back of his shoulder like it has been there before.

"Hold on," he says. Her hands are too small to reach around his ribs, so it's a stupid thing to say, but it's what you say.

"How fast?" she asks.

"Fast," he says.

"Good."

She is the only new weight he is carrying, and the only one he means to bring all the way home. The bike turns over and catches.

The first mile is gray zone. Hegewisch sprawl — no sovereign in residence, the infrastructure abandoned around 2180 and nobody come back to fix it. A dead delivery automaton kneels in a drainage lot on the corner, its chassis streaked chalk-white by years of rain. Some child has tied a festival ribbon around one outstretched hand, and the machine holds it patiently, the way it would hold anything, for as long as the ribbon cares to stay.

Stash had run a load through here last month and said the south stretch of Avenue O was clean if you took it fast. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> takes Avenue O at eighty. What light there is comes from the occasional working window, the phosphor glow of a sign that won't die, the reflected scatter of the city proper bleeding over the horizon. His neuretics compensate, painting the road in false color — the asphalt a darker gray, the potholes rendered as small dark wells.

Two rows of collapsed light poles lie across the road like felled trees. His neuretics finds the gap between them before he's had to think about it.

What Stash hadn't mentioned — what a month of rain and settling had done since — is the third pole, lying lengthwise inside the gap, hidden by the shadow of the first two until the last half-second. The neuretics has the line before he does. He lays the bike over far enough that the peg kisses wet asphalt, and the pole goes by close enough to smell the rust and the old paint and the ghost of whatever oil has been dripping down it for forty years, and then the road is just road again.

Imani's breath is a small warm patch against the back of his shoulder — even, slow, held on purpose.

"You're not scared," he says.

"I'm being efficient with my fear," she says.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> almost laughs. Then doesn't.

"Where'd you learn that?" he asks.

"The lady who got me ready. She said to say it until it's true."

"Is it true yet?" he asks.

Imani thinks about it and answers honestly. "No."

"Then keep saying it," he says.

title: Crucible Genomics
text:
The checkpoint is two guards in soft-helmet armor and a third tucked behind a blast-shield. All three wear the bored faces of men expecting a manifest. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> doesn't have a manifest. He has a child, a battery, and a smile — and he has learned that on the right night, with enough confidence, the three together pass for paperwork.

He brakes hard and throws both hands off the bars, palms open, a man holding nothing. He gets the words out before any of them finish reaching for a weapon.

"POST-OP TRANSIT," he shouts. "LACUNA COOLER. NORTHWESTERN."

The left guard looks at the brace. The right guard looks at the cooler's logo — reads it the way you read a shipping label, not a threat. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> keeps his voice flat, administrative, the tone of a man who has said these three words a hundred times and could not care less if he says them a hundred more. Impatience in the face, never fear. A courier doing his job.

The man behind the glass — Crucible internal, a white coat under his armor — lifts a handheld and aims it at Imani's face, because in a genomics zone the gate reads the person, not the plate. The bike is nobody here. The device takes its time, humming down past the surface, and whatever it gives him back drains the color out of his evening.

"Let him through," he says. "Phenotype clearance."

The barrier sinks into the road.

"Have a great evening," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says, and means it.

A mile and a half of Crucible private road — manicured, palm-lit, the river running black on the right. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pegs the throttle. Workers in beige smocks glance up from the greenhouses and decide not to look long. The kind of surface that costs money to maintain, laid down for people who belong on it. He doesn't, and he's accelerating anyway.

Imani's small weight settles against his spine as the bike finds its rhythm.

He thinks it through as he rides. The company has him tagged as a courier hauling inventory out. That's the only reason the gate opened, and it's only good while he keeps moving. Nobody who wants what's wired into Imani's chest can follow him through here — they don't carry whatever got him waved in. So they won't follow. Following would put them behind him, playing catch-up on a road he's already cleared.

They'll call ahead. Radios work faster than motorcycles. And the ones they wake on the far side won't need her breathing to collect, because a six-hour heart travels fine in a cooler.

He keeps moving.

"Why are the trees in rows?" Imani asks.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> follows her line. Cherry, he thinks, though the light is too low to be sure — planted in perfect symmetry down both sides of the road, a green tunnel that should be beautiful and reads instead as a calculation. Screening. A perimeter defined by aesthetics, so the wall doesn't look like a wall.

"Because the company likes to know where things are," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says.

"That seems anxious?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has nothing to add. The kid is right.

<entity repo="entertainment" guid="a3f7c2e1-b8d9-4f6a-0c5e-2d7b1a9f3c08">The Crucible</entity> gate rises and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> accelerates through before it's fully clear. Behind them, the checkpoint recedes into darkness—and then his neuretics catches something the bike's mirrors don't: motion on the roofline. A figure moving parallel to their trajectory, two hundred meters out, keeping pace with the tree-line.

Not a guard. Guards don't move like that.

"Still efficient with your fear?" he asks.

Imani doesn't answer right away. Her grip tightens on his coat.

"Starting to use some," she says.

The private road ends at a maintenance gate—the kind that opens for authorized vehicles and stays closed for everything else. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s courier credentials bought him the checkpoint. They won't buy him this. The gate is chain-link and motion-sensitive, and there's no time to cut it, no time to climb it, no time to ask it nicely.

He lays off the throttle and hits the turn toward the river instead.

The access road isn't a road anymore. It's gravel and standing water and the kind of terrain that kills bikes when they're moving fast. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> keeps moving fast anyway. The <entity repo="transportation" guid="8ce55923-24c2-4100-82dc-9ec3a9576c42">Aries Kimodo MDK</entity> is built for this—suspension tuned for impact, traction programming that reads the ground before the wheels touch it—but the margin between control and disaster is measured in centimeters now.

Imani's small sound—not quite a scream, not quite a laugh—tells him she's crossed the line from fear into something sharper.

The river path is narrow. On the left, the black water moves fast with recent rain. On the right, the tree-line they came through. Behind them, the figure on the roofline is gone, which means they've either lost him or he's repositioning. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics is picking up thermal signatures through the canopy—two of them now, maybe three, moving to intercept at the access bridge three kilometers ahead.

"How much farther?" Imani asks. Her voice is smaller now. The bravery is running thin.

"To the bridge or to Trauma Bay?"

"Either."

"Bridge is two minutes. Bay is forty-eight."

She processes this. "And after the bridge?"

"Open city. They can't follow without being seen."

"Will they follow?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> doesn't answer because the answer is yes and she already knows it. What she needs to know is whether they'll make it, and that's a different question entirely.

The bike's front wheel catches a pothole hidden by the water. The neuretics compensates before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s conscious mind registers the hit—a half-second of suspension adjustment, a minute correction in lean angle, the kind of automation that keeps a man alive when the alternatives are river or trees. Imani's fingers find his ribs through the coat and hold there.

"I'm not scared," she says. Automatic now. A prayer.

"You're doing fine," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says, and means it.

The access bridge is visible now—old steel, narrow, the kind of structure that was built forty years ago when nobody thought about what would happen if someone tried to cross it fast. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sees the first intercept point: a figure on the bridge itself, silhouetted against the far tree-line, hands raised like they're about to signal.

Not to signal. To fire.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> cuts hard left and drops the bike into the water.

The Aries doesn't sink. The H-Cell is sealed, the electronics hardened, the design philosophy built around *survive the impossible*. It also doesn't float, which means when the front wheel hits the river bottom and the back wheel follows, they're underwater for three long seconds that feel like thirty. Imani's grip becomes crushing. Her lungs are working. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics is screaming about the electrical load of the cooler, the battery, the wet systems trying to short out and fail.

Then the far bank rises up and the bike finds purchase and they're climbing out of the water into the tree-line on the far side of the bridge, the interceptor still trying to figure out what just happened, the thermal signatures behind them slowing to assess the crossing.

The bike sputters once and keeps running.

Imani is coughing water and laughing—actual laughter, the kind that comes after the moment of dying doesn't stick. "That," she gasps, "was not efficient."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. His hands are steady on the bars. His heart isn't. "That was the inefficient part."

"The heart," she says suddenly. Fear creeping back. "The cooler—"

"Sealed," he says. "Waterproof. The battery is the only thing that matters and it's rated for submersion."

Behind them, the bridge is already a quarter-mile away. The roofline figures are gone. The intercept team is reassessing. They have maybe sixty seconds before pursuit resumes, and by then <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> will have turned northeast toward the industrial corridor, where the surveillance grid is degraded and a fast bike can lose itself in the vertical sprawl.

"How many are chasing us?" Imani asks.

"Started with three. Now probably five."

"Are we going to make it?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> threads the bike between two massive ferrocrete pillars supporting the elevated highway above. The road narrows. The surveillance cameras here are older models, networked to systems that nobody's updated in five years—the seams where one corporate camera network ends and the next one's hasn't started, blind spots that exist because two territories couldn't agree on who paid for coverage in the gap between them. His neuretics reads those seams like a map, plots the rhythm of them: acceleration into the dead angle, a run through the alley the arc doesn't reach.

"Yes," he says.

"How do you know?"

Because I'm not done yet, he doesn't say. Because I've carried worse than this. Because the client needs you alive and I don't miss contracts.

What he says is: "Because we're still moving."

The bike banks hard into the industrial district, and the city opens up around them—vertical, dense, full of shadows deep enough to hide in. Behind them, the pursuit teams are still trying to cut off roads that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped using five minutes ago. They're looking for a motorcycle. He's looking for a gap. The distinction is the difference between the hunter and the hunted.

Imani's breathing settles. Her grip on his ribs eases from crushing to merely firm.

"The lady who got me ready," she says quietly. "She said if I ever had to run, run to someone who knows how. She said most people run like they're scared. But the ones who know—they run like they're already where they need to be."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> doesn't respond. He's too busy being exactly where he needs to be, which is a motorcycle moving through dark water and darker streets, carrying a child with a new heart and no legal right to keep it, toward a hospital that won't ask questions because the money will arrive before the questions get a chance to form.

<entity repo="entertainment" guid="a3f7c2e1-b8d9-4f6a-0c5e-2d7b1a9f3c08">The Crucible</entity> corridor recedes behind them. Ahead, the lights of Streeterville begin to appear—white and clean and impossibly far away.

"We're going to make it?" she asks again.

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. "We're going to make it."

title: The Pullman Seam
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a92d-7fda-a2d9-7ed2ca96fde4">Pullman Works</entity> glows up on the right — restored row houses, modern cameras hidden inside period fixtures, every window a registered occupant. An Axiom company town, keeping perfect time for people who don't own a single minute of it. The old ghost of total control, retrofitted and rented back to the tenants at a markup. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> threads the gray-zone seam along its edge, the unincorporated strip Axiom never bothered to fence — the space where the company's vertical-rights claim goes fuzzy and the surveillance density drops to something a person can move through without being catalogued. Where the factory rain has dried, the pavement has gone soap-slick, and he feeds the bike a little less lean through the stretch without thinking about it. The Aries reads the surface like braille, suspension adjusting under him three times a second, keeping the ride smooth over asphalt nobody maintains because nobody owns it.

Heads come up as the engine passes. One kid shouts something the engine swallows, but the shape of the word is unmistakable — legend — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> lifts a hand off the bars like a man in a parade.

Other heads come up too, and these ones don't spare a look for the bike. Fledglings. Pledges to the Vultures, the crews who strip the dead and the not-quite-dead for parts down in the deep gray where the Substrate has quit and nobody's coming to help. A fledgling runs salvage on spec — no patch, no blessing — hoping to drag home something worth a permanent place in the flock. They run warm, these ones, bodies hot with anticipation rather than exertion, the heat of a kid who thinks he's about to stop being nobody. A post-op transplant riding through open country isn't a target to a kid like that. It's a winning lottery ticket. The one score that carries you off the street and into the flock for good.

Two of them are already on their bikes. Already on their neuretics.

Imani's hand finds the side of his coat and grabs a fistful. She isn't afraid, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> realizes. She's taking it all in.

He had one job today: get her to the far side of the district in one piece, and keep her calm enough not to bolt before they got there.

"First time off the block?" he asks.

"First time on the ground," she says.

"Well," he says. "Buckle up."

"Buckle up to what?" she asks.

"Existentially," he says.

She thinks about that one for a long moment, the city pouring past on both sides of her—vendors under canopies that predate the aeroblocs and never bothered updating to match them, the ambient noise of a hundred transactions happening at once, foot traffic thick enough to swallow two people whole if you timed it right.

Then her grip on his coat goes rigid, and her feet stop. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turns. Two checkpoint marshals have peeled off the corner post and are angling toward them through the crowd, one already thumbing the reader on his belt, and the fistful of coat in Imani's hand is shaking now — not from fear of the ground anymore, but from the thing she's staring at over his shoulder.

The man is maybe thirty yards ahead, standing at a produce stall, examining fruit he has no intention of buying. Tall. Grey at the temples. The bone structure unmistakable if you're the person who inherited it. The thing that makes her whisper, "That's my father," and start pulling backward toward the exact bolt he'd promised himself she wouldn't make.

"Don't," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says quietly.

But she's already seen him. Her whole body has compressed into a single point, her breathing gone shallow, and every cell of her is screaming to turn around and run back into the one part of the crowd that would put her face and his in the same log line.

"Okay," she says, and when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turns them east into the thickest part of the crowd instead of away from it, she goes without another word— small, matching steps— the crowd closing behind them like water, filling the gap, obscuring the line of sight, until the shape she'd sworn was her father is thirty yards back and then gone, one more face the checkpoint line will never separately account for.

title: Ashgrave Corridor
text:
The <entity repo="place" guid="019e7d3d-ffca-74c5-a70b-760e2e72a274">Ashgrave Synthesis Corridor</entity> announces itself with a wall of haze you can taste a block before you can see it. The perimeter lights glow the wrong color — too yellow, too low — the way a refinery glows when it's brewing something. This is somebody's commute. A shift-change line of workers in cheap half-masks trudges the shoulder, heads down, lunch pails swinging, walking a thing they made peace with long ago, because the only other choice was not eating. A stall at the mouth of the corridor sells filter cartridges, and beside them a hand-painted board keeps a tally — DAYS SINCE — the number low, the way it's always low here.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has a respirator clipped to his jacket. Imani doesn't. His neuretics reads the air and shows him a number he doesn't like and a clock he likes even less — particulate count up forty percent, the display flags, <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> running a synthesis batch on the north end. He reaches back without slowing, finds her face with the flat of his palm, and presses his bandana over her mouth. It's not a mask. It's what you use when you didn't bring one for two, and he'd known that when he'd let her climb on.

"Breathe shallow," he says. "Through this. Not your nose."

She nods against his hand. A masked worker on the shoulder lifts two fingers as the bike passes — not a wave, just the nod one night-shift gives another across a bad stretch of road — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> returns it. Then he bites down on his own mouthpiece, snaps the seal, and rides into a sky the color of an old bruise like he was personally invited.

Fifty meters in, the shift-change line does what he doesn't expect: it stops moving forward and starts spilling sideways, into the road. Not for him — for a corridor checkpoint he can't see yet, a boom gate dropping across both lanes on hydraulics that sound like they're grinding bone, and a Synthesis foreman with a scanner wand waving the night-shift into a single choked column. The workers bunch up, masks turned toward the light, and the bike's clean lane vanishes into a wall of bodies and stalled bicycles. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> brakes and the tires chew grit. He can't gun through a crowd, and he can't stop — behind Imani's shallow breathing his neuretics ticks the exposure clock down in red, every idling second buying her lungs a dose he swore she wouldn't take.

The foreman is older, grey at the temples, his own mask looped around his neck — a man who's been breathing this air long enough it's stopped being a job and started being a fact of life. He thumbs the scanner and runs it across the frame first, the front wheel, the battery housing. The device chirps. Green light. Then the wand swings up, catches the bike, catches <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face, and holds there a beat too long, the way a scan holds when it's found something it was told to look for.

Two refinery towers breathe orange fire on either side of him, close enough that he could count the rivets if he had a second to spare. Sixty feet up, a vent stack blows down all at once, and the pressure slams sideways across the road. The bike yaws hard. He corrects before the yaw has finished, his hands moving a half-second ahead of the problem. Imani's grip tightens into a small steel claw at his belt.

"We're fine," he says, out loud.

And that's when the second stack lets go — behind them, out of sight, a low crump he feels in his sternum before he hears it. The road ahead unrolls a rippling wall of superheated air, and the bike doesn't yaw this time; it lifts, the rear wheel going light and loose the way it does right before it's gone entirely. He drops his weight, dumps throttle, feels the tire chirp and skate and finally, grudgingly, bite — but the correction costs him the line. They come out of it aimed at the wrong gap, the narrow service lane he'd been counting on now sliding past on his left as a chain-link gate swings shut across it on some automated timer he never knew existed. The clear road he'd been riding toward is simply not there anymore.

What's in front of them now is the eastern berm — a line of concrete tank traps, stacked and welded into a maze that's supposed to slow unauthorized traffic. It slows traffic. It doesn't stop it, not if you know where the gaps are, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knows this corridor. The bike drops into the first turn too fast. It leans and Imani's grip becomes a lock, and for half a second <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> feels the weight shift wrong — the center of gravity moving toward the outside of the turn instead of holding the line — and then her weight settles forward, and the bike straightens, and they're through. The heat at his back says whatever tripped those stacks is still tripping.

The second berm comes up faster. This one has a gap, but it's not a gap meant for bikes — it's a cut for foot traffic, a narrow slot between two massive concrete barriers, and it won't take them straight. So he doesn't take it straight. He leans into the approach, lets the front wheel kiss the edge of the left barrier, uses the contact to pivot the bike's angle — a move that should dump them both into the concrete and doesn't, because Imani shifts her weight forward at exactly the moment he needs her to, leaning into the turn like she's been riding behind dangerous men her whole life instead of three hours. The barrier scrapes chrome, a sound bright and terrible and gone in an instant.

"I know," she says through the bandana. "I can tell from your shoulders."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has met grown adults — armed, paid, supposedly professional — who couldn't read his shoulders. He is starting, against every instinct he owns, to take this kid personally.

Halfway through, the corridor's throat starts to close.

A leak somewhere upwind trips a containment lockdown, and <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity>'s answer to a leak is a blast-rated bulkhead coming down across the only open lane on a dead-man timer — slow as a guillotine, and about as open to argument. It's built to seal whoever's caught on the wrong side in with the air they were trying to outrun. This is not the sally-gate. There's no actuator to find and shoot, no override, and no time to look for one. A hydraulic spine already in motion is a different animal than one sitting at rest, and his neuretics tells him so before he's even finished the thought.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> can't beat the door. He can only beat it there.

He drops two gears and pins the throttle. In his skull the shrinking gap gets measured against the height of a man lying flat with a child folded down his spine, and the answer comes back with no margin anywhere in it. He takes it anyway. Something behind his eyes lurches — a warning, one full second of it while he leans that hard on the neuretics — then steadies.

The bike surges into the red, and the lane unrolls beneath them in a single stretched moment — concrete, warning paint, the shadow of the descending edge racing ahead of them like a blade falling. Imani's grip goes from steel claw to something beyond it, both fists locked in his coat, her whole body rigid against his back. The bulkhead is a wall now, dropping faster, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> doesn't rise so much as compress — his weight shifting forward, his body folding down against the tank, feeding the machine everything it has left.

They go under the falling edge at speed. The lip catches the battery brace and shrieks the whole length of it in a fan of orange sparks — a hand's width higher and the night ends here, for both of them — and then the bulkhead seats home behind them with a boom he feels in the floor of his chest. Through. He throws one look at the brace. Still green. The cooler held.

Imani isn't laughing this time. Both fists are buried in his coat, her face pressed flat between his shoulder blades, and she has gone very, very quiet. One more thing tonight has taught him about her.

He clears the corridor's north ramp at a hundred and ten, rolls off the throttle on the way down, and spits the mouthpiece out so it swings free on its lanyard. Reaching back one-handed, he tugs Imani's bandana down off her face.

"You with me?" he asks.

She coughs once, twice — the kind that comes out of a body just finished being wrong about dying — then says, "I'm with you. Your shoulders said we were okay."

"My shoulders are working overtime," he says.

"Give them a raise."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> laughs — a real one, surprised out of the bottom of him — laughs so hard he nearly loses the line. The road here is older than the refinery's patched asphalt, poured concrete gone smooth from a thousand shift changes and never swept, never worth sweeping, and the grit of all those years has settled down into the grain where the light won't show it.

The front wheel skips off the lip of a seam he never saw. Not far — a foot, maybe less — but at this speed a foot is a conversation. The bars kick sideways, wrenching against his grip. He fights it, muscles the tank between his knees, but the back end steps out on the loose grit and starts to come around, the rear wheel chasing the front like it's trying to catch up to a decision already made. Imani's weight lurches high on his spine, pitching them toward the wall he was supposed to be threading past — a tank berm, rust-stained, solid as a promise, and suddenly very close.

And the throttle, dead in his hand a second ago, won't answer clean when he twists it, coughing on something in the line.

title: Englewood
text:
The bike comes around hard, the rear wheel hunting for purchase on nothing but loose fill and intent. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hauls the front end up and over the skid, fighting the bars through three full rotations of counterlock before the chassis finally remembers how to track straight. The wall slides past his left knee close enough to read, and Imani's grip has gone rigid again—not fear this time, but the locked-down silence of someone who has decided to trust the body in front of her more than the ground underneath.

They've got maybe two hundred meters of open straightaway before the viaduct proper starts again, the concrete ramp that locals braced up after the collapse. The bike settles. The engine stops coughing. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> feeds throttle in measured increments, because any sudden movement right now will have her nerves doing gymnastics she doesn't deserve.

Behind them: headlights. Three sets, closing in a loose wedge formation.

The neuretics tags them before his eyes do—two civilian sedans and something heavier in the middle, the weight signature of a Synthesis freight runner with reinforced bumpers. Not police. Not Axiom. The formation is too clean, the timing too sharp. <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity> doesn't move on impulse, and this is <entity repo="character" guid="019dd276-fb32-7130-bba7-08604333865f">Hua</entity>'s reach.

"Company," he says.

"How long?" Imani's voice has gone flat, all the earlier warmth stripped out.

"Thirty seconds before they're close enough to matter."

The ramp starts its incline. The concrete is pitted and uneven, each seam a small betrayal waiting to throw the front wheel. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> takes it at a speed that would get him killed on a normal road, but this isn't a normal road—it's a structure that's already failed once and been held together by whatever the locals could afford. Rebar threaded through drilled slabs, load spread across pillars that bleed orange oxide down their flanks like old blood, the whole span stabilized by nothing but weight and time. Every crack tells him something about load distribution, about where the original slab is still bearing weight and where it's being carried by jury-rigged support. The bike's suspension works with that geometry, not against it.

The first sedan tries to follow. It makes it halfway up before its suspension bottoms hard enough that he hears the compression from fifty meters ahead. The driver corrects, loses momentum, and falls back. Smart money would stay back. This driver apparently isn't taking smart money.

The freight runner and the second sedan keep coming.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> leans hard into the geometry of the next seam, using the lip to bleed speed without touching the brakes. The bike responds—a slight drift, a moment of weightlessness that would terrify most riders. Imani shifts her weight with it, riding the lean like she's been doing this for years instead of minutes. His shoulders aren't the only thing getting a read tonight.

"Thirty meters," she says. "The freight runner is faster than the other one."

"You know vehicles?"

"I know *fast*."

The ramp crests and the far side drops away—not sheer, but close. The collapsed section opens up below them like a mouth. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has maybe four seconds to find a line through the broken concrete, find it clean, and commit to it without hesitation. Hesitation is what gets you pinned under a quarter-ton of machinery.

He sees it: a shelf of concrete, tilted at maybe twenty degrees, that runs diagonal across the fall. It'll work if he hits it exactly wrong—if he hits it exactly right, the angle will shed the bike's momentum and buy him distance. If he hits it anywhere else, they're tumbling.

He takes it at full throttle.

The impact comes up through his spine, his wrists, the base of his skull. The bike goes light—completely light, wheels off ground—and for one long breath they're flying. Then the rear tire catches the concrete shelf and the world inverts. Not a flip, just a hard rotation around the contact point, the bike's nose coming up and over and his stomach following two beats behind. Imani has stopped breathing entirely.

They land hard enough that the shock compressor in his wrist sends a spike of pain straight up his arm. The bike settles. The engine catches and holds. He corrects the line with one hand while the other reaches back to find Imani's grip still locked, still committed.

"Still with me?"

"You're insane," she says. It comes out like a prayer.

"Probably."

The freight runner crests the ramp. It's heavier, less nimble. The driver tries the same line <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took and realizes too late that the physics aren't going to work the same way. The truck's weight carries it off the shelf at the wrong angle. It doesn't flip—not quite—but it comes down hard enough that the suspension compresses and doesn't come back up the same way it went down. The driver wrestles it back onto the straightaway, but the alignment is shot and the front end is pulling hard to the right.

The second sedan has already given up. Brake lights are receding.

The freight runner keeps coming, limping but committed. Its driver is either brave or working on a contract that doesn't allow for failure. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s money is on the second one.

He leans forward, reading the road ahead. The straightaway ends at a junction where three possible routes split off—left into a warehouse district, right toward the industrial corridor, or straight into a tangle of surface streets that might lead somewhere useful or might lead nowhere at all. His neuretics has mapped the area enough to know that left is a dead end, right feeds into Axiom territory, and straight is the only option that doesn't end with him pinned down for a conversation he doesn't want to have.

The freight runner closes the gap to fifteen meters.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drops the bike's speed just enough to make the turn tight, then accelerates hard on the exit. The maneuver is designed to do one thing: force the pursuit to make a choice between following the line or hitting the corner too hot. The freight runner's driver chooses wrong. The truck's momentum carries it through the intersection at an angle, and the front bumper catches the corner of a loading dock. Metal screams. The truck bounces off the obstacle and comes back into the street, but it's bleeding pieces now—bumper, a section of the fender, something heavier that sparks when it drags.

The driver doesn't stop. The truck comes on again, slower now but still committed.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> takes the straightaway at full speed, Imani's weight steady against his spine, the neuretics running hot behind his eyes from the accumulated g-forces and the sustained attention. His heart rate holds at a metronome's beat, steady as a machine, because the wetware won't let it be anything else. Useful. Terrible. The truck is falling back now—damage compounding, physics finally winning the argument. By the time they reach the boundary of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>, it's three blocks behind and getting smaller.

He doesn't ease off the throttle until the truck's headlights disappear entirely. Only then does he let the bike slow, let the engine settle into something like a normal operating temperature, let the weight of what just happened settle into the places where adrenaline used to be. The air changes on this side—thinner, colder, carrying standing water and industrial runoff and the particular loneliness of a place nobody's supposed to be. The atmospheric processors don't reach this far down. The Substrate coverage goes patchy. It's the kind of place where you can disappear if you know how.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> does. He takes three turns without thinking, muscle memory and neuretics reading the street like a map he's been studying his whole life.

"We're clear," he says.

Imani is still gripping his coat. When she finally speaks, her voice is smaller than before. "What happens now?"

"Now we find <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. "And we don't tell her about any of this."

"She's going to know."

"My shoulders are going to lie," he says. "And this time, they're going to make it stick."

They come in a flock this time — the ones a ping woke, fresh bikes and no patience between them, fanning out across both lanes to take him at speed. The lead pair don't reach for guns. They reach for their belts and throw, and the air ahead of him fills with fat little cylinders that burst into white glare and dead static. Flashbang. Chaff. And the ugly third kind — the EMP and interference rounds a salvage crew carries to kill a mark's bike out from under him and blind whatever he's running behind his eyes.

It's a good plan. It would work on almost anyone alive.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s bike stumbles, coughs, catches, and keeps running on hardened ignition. And his neuretics never so much as flickers, because a military rig is shielded against far more than static. Against EMP. Against the whole spectrum of battlefield interference. And against the low, wrong pressure at the very bottom of the band — the kind that would fold a civilian rig clean in half. You don't harden a mind against that last thing unless you already know, for a fact, that it's out there waiting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has never told a living soul that his is. Where a pack of fledglings came by rounds that carry it is a question for a later night.

He stops the bike. Running is the one thing they're built for; standing still is the one thing they're not. He picks the narrow place under the 63rd Street viaduct, where the lane necks down between two dead cars, thumbs the bike into auto-balance, and feels it take its own weight — the gyros holding it upright and patient at a crawl, the kid still aboard.

"Don't move," he tells her.

<entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> goes still as furniture.

Then he steps off into the road and draws <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> off his back.

The first one commits to his swing — a length of chain, whipping flat — before he understands the whole fight just changed shape. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reads the arc early, the way he reads everything, and simply isn't where it lands. The chain's tail still opens a thin red line across his forearm, the tax for standing in this close. He takes that. On the same motion he pulls the rider off his bike, cuts the bandolier of grenades from his chest, and tosses it back underhand.

"Hold these."

<entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> catches it against herself like a schoolbag.

The second one tries to run him down, which is how the second one comes to study the asphalt up close. The third has the sense to draw a pistol — and that's the moment the neuretics shows him the thing no briefing can ever quite sell: the shot itself, a full beat before the trigger finishes pulling it, a hard red line laid from the muzzle straight through the center of his chest.

So <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> takes his chest off the line. He drops his weight back off his heels, far enough to feel the round part the air just above his sternum and travel on to find the fourth fledgling — who'd done everything right tonight except stand directly behind the man he was hunting. The shooter stares at what his own hand just did. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> relieves him of the pistol, and of any further interest in the fight.

The rest of the flock reads the odds and doesn't like them. Two peel away north and don't look back. The ones already on the ground will walk home when their legs come back around to the idea.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> swings onto his bike — still upright, still warm, still holding <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> exactly where he left her — kills the balance, and lets the weight settle into his hands like something he was born holding. <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> is looking down at the bandolier in her lap.

"Are these ours now?" she asks.

"Until some bigger kid wants to try and take them," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says, threading her free hand back through the back of his coat.

She thinks about that and finds it fair — which is, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> suspects, the most truthful thing anyone has ever bothered to tell her. He brings them back up to speed, and for the first time since Pullman the mirrors stay empty behind him. They are done being chased.

title: The One Who Doesn't Stop
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">The Gray Zone</entity> boundary posts blur past—old concrete teeth set in a line that nobody officially acknowledges and everybody knows not to cross wrong. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> threads between them at a speed that looks casual and isn't, Imani's hand locked in his coat, the bandolier of grenades riding in her lap like the most dangerous homework assignment in the city.

The bike settles into a normal pulse once they clear the posts. His neuretics still singing that high, wrong note—the one that comes after the body runs hotter than it's supposed to for too long. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aab8-7e48-97ef-8183dc295aba">Heat</entity> behind his eyes. Pressure at the base of his skull where the array connects. The EMP rounds didn't touch him, but they touched *something* on the way past, some harmonic he didn't know he was carrying.

"How far to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s?" Imani asks. Her voice is steadier now. The fear is still there—it's just learned to share space with curiosity.

"Two kilometers. Carousel junction, then south through the old park."

"The carousel is still running?"

"Still running," he says. "Has been for forty years. The city changes around it and it keeps going."

He takes the turn onto Halsted at a pace that lets the bike settle into its own rhythm. The street here is mixed—gray-zone nominally, but close enough to the boundary that Axiom surveillance drones make regular passes. Enough to keep the worst of the predators honest. Not enough to stop them entirely.

The carousel appears like it always does: sudden, anachronistic, lit from underneath by lights that have been running so long they've become part of the streetscape. The horses are faded to a uniform gray-brown by two centuries of weather. The music box mechanism still turns, playing something that might have been a waltz once, before the gears got loose enough to make it sound like something dying in slow motion.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> slows the bike. Not stopping—stopping draws attention. But slowing enough that Imani can see it, can take the measure of the thing.

"It's beautiful," she says.

He doesn't argue. The carousel is beautiful the way a scar is beautiful—evidence of something that survived past the point where survival was supposed to end.

The road curves past it, and that's when his neuretics catches the wrong frequency.

It's not loud. It's not the shrieking EMP band or the interference static the fledglings threw at him. It's underneath everything—a bass note at the very bottom of the perceptual band, so low it's almost a feeling rather than a sound. His implant flags it at 17 Hz. Maybe 18. The exact band where the carousel's music box mechanism sits, where the old infrastructure breathes. He knows this frequency. He's catalogued it. The city generates it in patches, usually near the old schism sites, usually in places where the geometry got bent and never quite straightened back out.

Except the carousel isn't the source.

The source is coming from *under* the carousel. From the junction beneath the park. From something that just woke up or just arrived or just decided this was the moment to start singing.

His hand tightens on the throttle. Imani feels it—the bike's acceleration is immediate and unconcealed.

"What?" she says.

"Schism," he says. Not a question. A confirmation of what his hardware is already telling him. The numbers tick upward like a countdown to something he hasn't been briefed on—18.2 Hz, 18.5—and the sensation shifts from pressure to something closer to presence. A weight in the back of his skull his implant is trying very hard to parse into something useful. It runs the signal through the tactical filters, the environmental mapping, the threat assessment protocols. Nothing. Not a weapon signature. Not municipal infrastructure. Not Axiom's sensor grid. Not the atmospheric processors running their endless redistribution cycles. Something down there in the substrate beneath the city just opened its eyes.

"How bad?"

He doesn't answer because the answer depends on the next five seconds. Depends on whether the thing stays under the carousel or decides to follow. Depends on whether Imani's weight on the bike is enough to drag his attention away from the road or whether he can hold both things at once—the path in front of him and the wrongness climbing through the spectrum behind.

The bike accelerates past the point where casual looks plausible. They're running now, and they're running hard, and the carousel is already getting smaller in the mirrors.

The frequency doesn't follow. It stays centered on the junction. Stays singing underneath the old music box. Stays *there*.

But it doesn't resolve. It doesn't fade back to baseline the way a normal schism micro-bleed should—distance doing its work, the signal degrading as they move out of whatever pocket of wrongness generated it. That's what should happen. That's not what happens.

It just keeps climbing. 19.1. 19.3. The resonant frequency of the 5D substrate itself, the one that every active schism membrane rings at when something down there is paying attention.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands have gone white on the throttle.

"It's not chasing us," Imani says. Not a question either. She's reading him the way he reads the road.

"No."

"It's doing something else."

"Yes."

He doesn't slow down. Not yet. But the mirrors tell him what he already knows—the carousel is far enough behind now that they're outside the immediate bleed radius. The frequency plateaus at 19.4 Hz and holds there, steady, like something tuning itself to a specific pitch and deciding to stay. Not rising with his speed. Not fading with the distance. Anchored to a point in the city he's already moving away from, and it doesn't care that he's moving. It's not tracking him—that's the thing his implant finally flags as significant. Not a proximity warning, not a proximity field. Just *there*, patient and fixed, broadcasting into the space where he used to be.

He's never heard of a signal that does that.

His array is screaming warnings he doesn't have a framework for. Military hardening doesn't mean immunity. It means he can *hear* the thing trying to talk to him through the substrate, can feel it the way you feel a <entity repo="place" guid="8b24a5eb-e8c2-8de1-fe67-f2d0ea0bd53e">low frequency</entity> through your ribs, and he still has to keep the bike upright and Imani breathing and the both of them moving toward a destination that suddenly feels a lot farther away than two kilometers.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s," Imani says quietly. "Still the plan?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> downshifts through a corner, the bike leaning into the turn with the same precision it's been showing him for three years. The carousel is gone now. The frequency is not.

"Still the plan," he says.

But his shoulders have already started lying. They're doing it so smoothly he almost believes them himself.

title: The Cinderfall Anomaly
text:
Halsted north of the tracks runs straight over the bones of Cinderfall Energy — eleven underground thermal plants whose only face to the world is a grid of steam-vent grates and the heat-waves rippling up off them, bending the streetlights into water.

"Why is the air doing that?" Imani asks.

"Because the company underneath us is cooking," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says.

"Oh." Then, smaller, all the cleverness gone out of it: "I don't like it here."

"Me neither," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says, and doesn't dress it up, because that one is simply true.

He doesn't tell her that the air is about to do something Cinderfall has nothing to do with. With the road behind him finally empty, his neuretics has nothing left to track but what waits ahead — the power-blue cones marking the perimeter already catching his headlight, holo tape looping between them on three sides, Halsted left open on the fourth because nobody was going to close Halsted for one of these. Municipal-grade cones, the kind that get deployed for hazmat containment, except there's no work crew, no vehicles, no sign explaining what they're keeping in or what they're keeping out. The ambiguity is the whole point. Two blocks on, the streetlights stop agreeing about where they stand. And the read in his skull, which has had a clean answer ready for everything tonight, goes quiet. In the array's running log, the 18.7 Hz notation that's been running since the carousel — type: unclassified, action: none, no category, a month of it — drops out. No transmission from the source end. Just gone. Quiet in the one specific way that means only one thing.

The Weather, Pike had called it.

He eases the bike back, meaning to put the perimeter behind him — and the wheel gives him nothing. Not a skid, not a slide; the road simply stops being a place where turning around is a thing that happens. The headlights find the power-blue cones again, dead ahead, closer than they were a breath ago. Behind him, where empty Halsted should be, his mirrors show the same cones, the same looping tape. Whatever direction he faces is the direction that leads in. The city's noise compresses with them, like someone turned the volume down on everything outside the perimeter and forgot to turn it back up. And behind him, Imani has gone very still, her hand finding the collar of his coat, because she has felt it too — that they are no longer approaching the perimeter. They are inside it, and it is closing the fourth side that nobody was ever going to close.

He should turn west. West is Bridgeport, and Bridgeport is normal. He goes straight, because straight is where the call is.

At 35th and Halsted the air changes temperature with nothing anywhere to explain it — a dry, settled cold, and under the cold the smell of a room sealed shut since before he was born. The world quietly stops being a place. The headlight reaches out and touches something, and the something touches back. The edges of everything go dim. His stomach drops and doesn't come back. The wheels are still on pavement, but the pavement is running half a second behind where his eyes swear it should be.

His neuretics read it first, the way the array is built to. The lamp on the corner should be three meters north and it isn't. It's where it was before. Where it will be after. The hardware flags the reading as impossible and keeps running the same calculation, looking for the error in itself, finding none. His hands know what to do without asking him — keep the throttle steady, keep the bike upright, keep moving, because stopping is the thing that kills you in a space that doesn't work.

And then comes the worse thing. The thing the briefings never sell hard enough.

He knows this corner.

The neuretics hands him a location stamp from a source with no registry entry — a fragment marked *origin: external, classification unknown, timestamp corrupted*. Not a memory. Not a file pulled from the city's infrastructure. Something surfacing in the wet-dark part of the array that doesn't have a name, arriving like data he downloaded years ago and forgot he had. The hardware flags it and waits. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has no category for it.

He has never once been here, and he knows it anyway — the way you know a hallway from a dream you've had your whole life and never once on purpose. At the near edge of the perimeter a structure stands that his headlight sweeps past in half a second. The angle of its face is a thing his skull already holds, curb to door, the precise distance, the way the streetlight ought to bend its shadow. He does not look at it.

The thing has a name on the weather forecasts and a warning flag on the maps. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knows the names are just manners. It isn't bad air. It isn't radiation. It is something aware of him — faintly, and in no hurry.

His neuretics try to map it and hand him nothing but garbage. Distances that won't sit still. A clock running three ways at once. His own engine note reaching his ears a half-second late, off a street he already left. The picture in front of him sits a little ahead of itself, like a page turned early. The buildings stand where they should, but their shadows fall the wrong way. Light from a window two floors up hits his eyes a moment before he passes it.

So he flies on the one instrument no upgrade ever beat: the old animal at the base of his skull.

He picks one streetlamp far out on the rim and holds to it. Sodium-orange, steady, three blocks north, anchored to a pole that hasn't moved. Not the road. Not the mirrors. Not the thing his array is failing to parse. The lamp.

Constant speed. Eyes on the light. Don't look at the edges. Don't trust a turn — in here, right is sometimes left, and left is sometimes down.

He eases the throttle forward, holding the line. The neuretics is still screaming, but he's learned to drive through screaming — learned it the way a body learns anything, by doing it until the panic becomes just another instrument reading. The streetlights on either side are no longer aligned. They flicker at different phases, a strobe his neuretics tries to lock onto and can't. His eyes water. He doesn't blink. Looks at the lamp.

The lamp doesn't get closer the way lamps should. It stays three blocks off, which means the distance is holding, which means he's matched whatever the Weather is doing. The pavement beneath the front wheel catches a seam, a discontinuity, and the bike shudders — just enough to remind him the road is still physical, still real even on a delay no augmentation can compensate for.

The air feels full. It feels like a room where something huge and very old has just turned around to look at you. Not angry. Just patient, like it has all the time there is. The frequency in his skull settles — not climbing, settling, like something that was waking up has finished and is now only watching. The kind of old that stopped being young before years were invented.

The buildings on either side begin to exist in more than one place at once, edges blurring at angles that shouldn't be possible, windows showing rooms lit from sources that aren't there. He doesn't look at the rooms. Doesn't acknowledge them. Keeps the lamp centered and the bike moving at the speed it's held since they entered this — the only thing in here still obeying the laws he knows.

"Don't look left," he says.

"Okay," Imani says. Her voice comes out thin. Her hand finds his coat, grabs a fistful, and stays there.

At the edge of his vision something moves that shouldn't be able to. A shape with one shadow too many — and the extra shadow arrives a half-beat ahead of the shape that throws it. Where it passes, the air goes cold with no source, and it makes no sound, only a pressure in the ear like water at depth.

He does not look straight at it. Some animal part of him knows a mind doesn't come back from looking straight at that. Imani's breath catches against his back — his only warning — and he throws the bike right, though right is the wrong word for the direction it actually goes. The miss should have cleared a foot. It clears less than an inch. He feels it pass like a current turning in deep water, and a line of cold opens along his ribs under the coat — deep, clean, not bleeding yet, because in here the blood runs a half-second behind everything else.

Then the far lamp swims up close and steady and yellow. The pavement grabs his tires all at once. The engine note folds back into itself and becomes an engine again. The cold line under his ribs catches up and burns now, the way real wounds burn once the blood arrives. He does not look back. He rides.

And behind him, the borrowed calm finally breaks. Imani comes apart — all the way apart, the way an eight-year-old does — sobbing into his back, both small fists twisting in his coat. "It looked right at me, it looked right at me, I want to go home, I want to go home." The brace at his kidney picks it up and starts to chirp, fast and climbing, because a six-hour-old heart was never built to run this hard. That, and not the thing back in the dark, is what can kill her now.

Keep her calm, Pike had said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has no calm left and no time to fake any, so he gives her the only thing he has — his voice, flat and low and dull as a machine reading off numbers. Not reassurance, which is a lie, but facts, which are the only thing that still holds shape out here.

"The lamp ahead is mercury vapor," he says. "There's a bird nest in the housing. You can see it if you look straight at the lamp. Don't look anywhere else." He eases the throttle. "The bike weighs three-forty. You weigh maybe sixty. The road's holding both of us across two contact patches the size of my hand. The road will hold."

The chirp keeps climbing.

"Your heart's running fast. That's your body answering something it doesn't have a name for. Count it," he says. "One, two, three. Keep counting. That's you, still here. Everything else is noise."

She counts. Her voice is barely there, but it's there. The bridge comes up. The loud part she likes.

"You're out of it. It's behind us. It can't come where we're going."

The chirp slows. Slows again. Steadies. By the next block she has herself back, mostly, in the wrung-out way a kid does after the worst of it lets go.

"You're hurt?" she asks, very quietly.

He can feel the wound bleeding in earnest now, a slow warmth soaking into the waistband, the kind that will need pressure and a clean table soon. His hand stays white on the throttle.

"I'm fine," he says.

It is the first time he has lied to her.

Twenty-one minutes, and the mirrors have stayed empty since the viaduct. What he still has is the Loop — the one part of the city no CorpoNation gets to switch off. Too public, too packed. It's the heart every zone plugs into to stay alive. So when it goes wrong, it goes wrong in the open. Tonight it is going wrong.

He hears it from the mouth of the tunnel: the flat clap of small-arms under a crowd's roar. Not the ragged noise of a riot — three-round bursts, disciplined spacing, the sound of money spending ammunition at a rate the municipal side can't match. Imani lifts her head off his back.

"Is that the loud?" she asks, a thread of the schism still in her voice.

"Different loud," he says. "Just people."

The long way costs eleven minutes he's already bleeding through, so he goes in. Halfway down the dark, a corporate security line has a municipal picket pinned behind an overturned cleaning rig. Both sides are too far gone to notice a motorcycle until it's the most interesting thing in the tunnel. The acoustics turn every shot into a chorus — a round cracks off a support column, another punches a neat exit hole through the ferrocrete three feet ahead, and there's no telling which direction any of it came from. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> uses that. He reaches back, and Imani presses a flashbang into his hand before he can ask. He throws it with his sword arm. It hits the ceiling and goes off. The tunnel goes white, and he rides the median straight through the blind seconds — and one of those frightened people gets lucky. A round tears a hot line across the top of his shoulder and nearly rips the gun out of his hand. Clean furrow, no bone, just the specific burning of a bullet passing close enough to char. He keeps the throttle. Adds the shoulder to the rib.

Behind them the two lines open up again, each side now certain the other just tried something, and by the time anyone thinks to aim at a motorcycle the deeper dark has swallowed it. Imani watches the rivers of light pour past overhead, not the blood she can't see.

"It's beautiful," she says.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gets his breath back around the burn before he answers, so it comes out level.

"Don't tell the advertisers," he says. "It'll go to their heads."

<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-183b-7977-b5ab-a0260fcb4086">River</entity> North is a thirty-second wedge of gray zone where the Loop's grid loses its nerve at the river. The old lift bridges are still there, but nobody has managed the river in eighteen years. The lift machinery seized a decade back, so the spans sit down for good, half-drowned. Lower Wacker is a black canal under them now, where a road used to run. People live here anyway — laundry strung span to span, a man fishing the canal off a fixed deck with a hand line, a kid working a cooler of something cold down a line of cars that never moves. Down a stairwell that runs below the waterline, a crack in the wall gives off a faint blue-green light, the way the oldest blocks do once they've been wet long enough. The air coming up out of it is cold and close and smells of a cellar that has made its peace with the river.

<entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> turns to watch the water slide past underneath. "The street's drowned," she says — not scared, just taking it in.

"Most of them down here are," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says. He takes the upper deck of the Michigan Avenue span, where <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7b5-7b46-81ed-0060cae29ca4">Tollgate Systems</entity> strung a credit-gate across a public ruin, because someone always finds a way to charge rent on a thing nobody owns. He doesn't have a Tollgate badge. He has twelve minutes and an opinion about Tollgate. The barrier is a swinging steel boom. It folds off its hinge without complaint — the least dangerous thing to happen to him all night.

What he thinks about instead is the camera reading his face across the span. Not the bike — the bike is nobody. It's him the system wants, and it bills the only name it can match: a credit account that hasn't existed since 2207, one he built for exactly this kind of night and then deleted. The charge will bounce. The rejection will get filed, archived, and wiped in a routine sweep. Six weeks and seventeen quanta of Tollgate's money, all chasing a ghost. He laughs, and it pulls at the cold line under his coat.

"Why are you laughing?" <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity> asks.

"Because the most expensive thing I did to them tonight was the paperwork."

"Good," she says.

But the charge doesn't bounce. Halfway across the span the boom behind them swings back up and locks — and the one ahead drops flat across the deck, boxing them onto the half-drowned span. A voice crackles from the camera housing, flat and pleased: "Account matched. Welcome back, Mr. Reyes. We've been holding this line open six weeks waiting for you to use it." The ghost account he deleted was never dead. Someone kept it breathing as bait, and he rode straight onto the hook — twelve minutes gone, both exits sealed, and a dead name spoken aloud in a place he can't get out of.

title: Streeterville
text:
He'd put the bike through the second boom the same dumb way he'd put it through the first—the lock only held current, not force, and eighteen years of neglect didn't care what the account said—and left Tollgate arguing with an empty span behind him.

Streeterville is a forest of glass towers wearing crowns of advertising, and at their feet sits the gray concrete slab of Northwestern Memorial. Tonight the whole district is packed wall to wall. The strike has spilled north into the one part of the city nobody is allowed to lock down — which is exactly why the strike came here.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picks out the bay's red light six blocks off. Between him and it, wading through the crowd on six legs with the patience of a thing that has nowhere better to be, is an <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> crowd-control unit. A crab the size of a panel van, matte riot-grey. A Bulwark. <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> builds everything into a crab in the end — low, wide, impossible to tip over — and a crab, it turns out, is what has been waiting at the end of his night.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> has put this exact unit down twice before. He knows it's the same one, because it slows the instant its optics find his face, recalculates, and comes for him first out of a crowd of a thousand easier problems.

A machine can't hold a grudge. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped believing that the second time.

The Bulwark is built to work shoulder to shoulder with civilians, so it carries nothing that goes bang — no slugs, no rockets, nothing that doesn't care where it lands. What it has instead is hands. Tanglefoot. Kinetic foam. A sonic throw that turns your inner ear to surf. And four hydraulic claws built to fold a person up neat and hold them there for collection.
