The crowd parts for it the way water does — people screaming, people running, people filming it on their neuretics because the city has trained them that documentation is the only form of protest that survives collection. The Bulwark doesn't care. Its legs hit the pavement in a rhythm that doesn't vary. It wants <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> folded up. It doesn't care about the kid at all, except as part of the same package.

That is the opening. It's a thin one.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> works Imani's hands free of his coat without setting her down — she stays on the pillion, she stays with the bike — and pulls two fat cylinders from the bandolier she's carried since the viaduct. The fledglings' own flash and chaff. Finally good for something.

"It sees in light, and it hears in sound, and it can't shoot back," he says. "Left one's flash — that blinds it. Right one's chaff — that makes it deaf and stupid. Pull the tab, count two, throw it at the face."

Imani looks at the crab the size of a panel van. Then she looks at the two grenades in her own two hands.

"It's a really big crab?" she asks, in the voice of a kid who has just been handed the best and worst job of her short life.

"It is," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agrees. "Throw at the face."

She pulls the left tab. She counts — too fast, a kid's two, barely one — and she throws.

The flash goes wide. It skims off the Bulwark's shoulder plate and bursts against the wall behind it, and the wall goes white, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s own vision blows out to a screaming nothing — that hard, flat burn that erases everything, even through closed eyelids. His hand is already moving for the throttle he can no longer see. And the Bulwark, unblinded, unbothered, takes one patient step forward and folds a claw shut around the bike's front wheel — the wheel, the frame, the fork — pinning all three of them where they sit.

The chaff is still live in Imani's other hand, tab pulled, counting down, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> can't see it to take it from her.

Then everything is very loud and very fast at once.

The claw has all its patience on the wheel it just caught, four hydraulic fingers closing slow and sure around metal that isn't going anywhere — which means, for one half-second, nothing is watching the rest of the machine. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> throws his weight sideways and tears the frame out from under the claw's grip, leaving the wheel and fork behind in its fist, and goes under the Bulwark instead of away from it, because the one place a crab cannot reach is the spot beneath its own belly. He slings the two of them through the gap between its legs — three inches of clearance, maybe four, the machine too wide to tip so it sits low and never expects a man to choose the dark under its chassis — drawing <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> as the world tips sideways, and opens one leg clean on the way through. The blade doesn't cut so much as punch: carbon nanotube through steel through the hydraulic lines underneath, and the fluid comes out bright and hot across the pavement. The Bulwark drops a quarter of its height with a sound like a building deciding to sit down.

His left foot lands a half-inch outside where he aimed it, and he fixes it without knowing he's fixing it.

Then, for the first time all night, the edge fails him.

All night the schism has given him a half-second lead — a beat of warning before anything happened, his body arriving early. Now that lead runs out. He feels it like a missed heartbeat, a gap where the calculation should be and nothing but static in its place. The light in the corner of his eye flares red, the half-second doesn't come, and his body arrives late instead. His knee buckles half a step. For one full second he is only a tired man with a sword, slow as everyone else in the world.

So he never sees the claw. It whips back over the fallen flank, folds shut on the bandolier across Imani's chest — the whole load, grenades and ammunition and tools — and tears it loose, lifting her half a foot into the air before the strap gives and drops her hard.

Something bigger had wanted them. Exactly the way he told her it would.

But she'd pulled the chaff's tab a heartbeat before the claw took her, and the two-count runs out now — point-blank, in the crab's own grip, bursting right in the sensors the claw reached out with. The payload is small; grenades built for crowd control don't carry much. But it's in the machine's palm, and the machine can't let go. The legs stop agreeing with each other and start hunting for a floor that isn't there.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> gets her down behind the engine block and puts himself between her and the machine, and finishes it the slow way — on grip and memory alone, with nothing out in front of him. No more distance. No more speed he can't rely on. Just geometry and <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. The Bulwark's claws come at him in a panic sequence, not calculated, just desperate: he sidesteps the first, lets the second pass over his shoulder, moves inside the third. A claw widens the cut on his forearm. The bad rib tears on a blind pivot. He takes both, because he never saw them coming. That is the difference. He finds the seam where the claw's mounting plate meets the chassis, the hydraulic line already torn open and spraying, and drives <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> in and twists until the claw goes slack. He lets the machine commit its whole weight to the crush, and when it does — its center of gravity already wrong from the opened leg — it tips. The Bulwark folds down into the intersection, blind and deaf and beached, its legs working and going nowhere. The bike does not survive the dismount.

But the bay's red light is three blocks off now. And three blocks is nothing.

"Good count," he tells her.

Imani — shaking, fierce, wrung all the way out, staring at the claw that took her grenades and choked on them — says, "I know."

The bike is dead and the bay is three blocks off, and three blocks is nothing. He has bled a lot more than this for a lot less. He sheathes <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his back. Holsters <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> on his hip. Then he picks her up — harness, battery, the whole small weight of her gathered in against his chest.

<entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity>'s hand fists in his collar. "You're hurt," she says again, and this time he doesn't bother with the lie.

"Yeah," he says.

He carries her. Ahead, the red light grows larger and brighter.

Pike is already out in the lane with the gurney — tall, brown-skinned, hair tied back, scrubs hanging off a body that has clearly run a long way today. He doesn't waste a syllable on hello.

"On the gurney."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> is already lowering her onto it. The harness comes off in two practiced motions. <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-763e-7869-a03d-deddfdc43117">Imani</entity>'s hand stays knotted in his coat a half-second after the rest of her is down, and when he gently pries it loose, she asks him a hard question.

"Will I see you again?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> does not lie to her. He has been lied to by kinder people than himself, and it never once helped.

"No," he says. "Probably not."

His hands hang empty at his sides, no next move in them. He puts one back to work — the only work left that's his to do. Hand her clean to Pike, he tells himself. Whatever else this night takes, she leaves it whole. He sets his palm flat between her shoulder blades and steadies the small of her back against the gurney, easing her the last inch down into Pike's keeping, and does not let go until Pike's hand has taken the weight of her from his.

She takes it the way she has taken everything else tonight — straight, no flinch, tucking it away somewhere. Good, he thinks. Better now, while she's still young enough for the scar to set smooth. He learned it late himself.

"Thank you for the loud," she says.

"Anytime, kid," he says — the gentlest lie he has told all night, and the only one she lets him keep. "Tell the heart I said hi."

Pike reads the brace, the wires, the cooler — and then reads him. The hand pressed flat to his side. The dark spreading at the forearm and the shoulder. The boot that won't quite take his full weight.

"Fifty-two minutes," he says. "I had you at fifty-five."

"You bet against me?"

"I bet the over. Paid for the gurney you just put her on." Pike snaps his fingers twice at a trauma nurse, points at Imani, and the bay swallows her the way good bays do — fast, and from all sides at once. "Eleven years, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. You keep bringing me work in worse shape than the patients."

"I cheated," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> says.

"You're bleeding into my ambulance lane." Pike doesn't raise his voice. He never has to. His is the flat weight of a man who has already had this argument in his head and won it. "That's a through-and-through on your forearm, and your ribs are singing. I can hear it in your breathing from here. Stay. Half the people in my bay tonight are in better shape than you are."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wants exactly one thing now: to walk out of this bay under his own power before anyone can lay hands on him and make him a patient too. The cut on his forearm is a clean thing, a bleed that means nothing if you don't think about it, and he does not think about it. He glances at the gap between Pike and the door, measures it, decides he can make it.
